newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe sets growth at five percent in new plan.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe sets growth at five percent in new plan.

text.p: The Zimbabwe government is proposing a new reform programme emphasising greater public and private sector efficiency and aiming for economic growth of at least five percent annually over the next five years.
The five-year programme, called the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation (ZIMPREST) envisages domestic product (GDP) growth built on higher exports and domestic deregulation.

Zimbabwe's economy is expected to grow by seven percent this year, but GDP growth has averaged 0.6 percent annually between 1991 and 1995 and many local analysts see the five percent target as overly ambitious.

"The fundamental objective of ZIMPREST is to bring about an adequate and sustainable rate of economic and social development to eliminate poverty and create the basis for all of Zimbabwe's citizens to provide a better life for themselves and their children," says the 150-page ZIMPREST draft document, obtained by Reuters on Friday.
The government has kept the document under wraps, ignoring calls by Zimbabwean industrialists to circulate it widely to stimulate public debate before its adoption.
Industry leaders and unionists complain that the first economic structural adjustment programme (ESAP) which ended last year was adopted without debate or consultation.
The ZIMPREST document, which is being discussed by the government and international donors, is expected to form the basis of a second Western-backed ESAP to be launched later this year.
Zimbabwe embarked on the first ESAP in 1990 after a failed seven-year flirt with socialism. Economists say major strides were achieved in trade liberalisation and domestic deregulation.

But they say the government failed to meet fiscal targets resulting in an unstable macro-economic environment which led the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to suspend a $120 million in vital balance of payment support a year ago.
The government acknowleges these failures and pledges in ZIMPREST to reduce the budget deficit to three percent by the year 2000 from the projected 10.2 percent this fiscal year.

The document projects labour growth of over four percent per annum between now and the year 2000, and targets employment growth of over five percent annually, to reduce unemployment, currently estimated at around 50 percent, to under 24 percent by 2000.

New central bank and banking acts are expected to be in place before the start of the programme to ensure the smooth operation of a modern banking system. Monetary policy will continue to target inflation, currently running at 24.7 percent, way off the single digits envisaged under ESAP.
